Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) History specification, Issue 6

tiers: None (single tier, linear, all exams at the end of the course)

assessment.title: Thematic study and historic environment
assessment.content: Crime and punishment in Britain, c1000-present (thematic, 36 marks) with Whitechapel, c1870-c1900 (historic environment, 16 marks)
assessment.format: Section A historic environment: two knowledge questions and a two-part source question. Section B thematic: Questions 1 and 2 compulsory, choice of one of two for the last question. Up to 4 SPaG marks sit in the Section B extended answer.

assessment.title: Period study and British depth study
assessment.content: Period study: Superpower relations and the Cold War, 1941-91 (32 marks). British depth study: Early Elizabethan England, 1558-88 (32 marks)
assessment.format: Two booklets. Period booklet: four questions, 1-3 compulsory, choose two of three parts in Question 4. British depth booklet: four questions, 1-3 compulsory, choose one of two in Question 4.

assessment.title: Modern depth study
assessment.format: Section A: a source question and one question from a choice of two. Section B: one four-part question on two sources and two interpretations. Up to 4 SPaG marks sit in Question 3(d).

nonExam: None. There is no coursework or non-exam assessment; all three papers are sat at the end of the course.

aos.desc: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of key features and characteristics of the periods studied
Explain and analyse historical events and periods using second-order concepts
Analyse, evaluate and use contemporary sources to make substantiated judgements
Analyse, evaluate and make substantiated judgements about interpretations

units.title: Crime and punishment in Britain: c1000-c1500
points: Crimes against the person, property and authority, including poaching and the Forest Laws.
Enforcement through tithings, the hue and cry and the parish constable.
Punishment aimed at deterrence: fines, corporal and capital punishment.
Case study: Church influence, including sanctuary, benefit of clergy and trial by ordeal.
Factors to track throughout: attitudes in society, individuals and institutions, science and technology.

units.title: Crime and punishment in Britain: c1500-c1700
points: Heresy and treason as crimes against authority; new crimes of vagabondage and witchcraft.
Policing through town watchmen; transportation begins and the Bloody Code starts.
Case study: the Gunpowder Plotters, 1605.
Case study: Matthew Hopkins and the witch-hunts, 1645-47.

units.title: Crime and punishment in Britain: c1700-c1900
points: Highway robbery, poaching and smuggling; witchcraft prosecutions end.
Tolpuddle Martyrs as an example of crimes against authority.
Policing develops: the Fielding brothers, police forces and the CID.
Transportation, public execution and the Bloody Code end.
Prison reform by Howard and Fry.
Case studies: Pentonville prison and Robert Peel's reforms.

units.title: Crime and punishment in Britain: c1900-present
points: New forms of theft and smuggling; driving, race and drug crimes.
Neighbourhood Watch and specialist, scientific policing.
Abolition of the death penalty.
Open prisons, treatment of young offenders and non-custodial alternatives.
Case studies: Conscientious Objectors in both World Wars and the Derek Bentley case.

units.title: Whitechapel, c1870-c1900: crime, policing and the inner city
points: Local context: housing, overcrowding, the Peabody Estate, workhouses and links between environment and crime.
Inhabitants: poverty, unemployment, lodging houses, pubs and migration, including Jewish migration in the 1880s.
Policing: the beat constable, H division, rookeries and attacks on Jewish people.
Investigative policing: detective methods, jurisdiction problems and the Jack the Ripper case with press coverage.
National context: the Metropolitan Police, CID, the Home Secretary, Sir Charles Warren and public attitudes.
Source skills: using local and national sources and judging their strengths and weaknesses.

units.title: Superpower relations and the Cold War: origins, 1941-58
points: Early tension: the Grand Alliance, Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam, ideology, the atomic bomb and Soviet satellite states.
Development: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Cominform, Comecon, NATO and the Berlin Crisis.
Intensification: the arms race, the Warsaw Pact and the Hungarian Uprising.

units.title: Superpower relations and the Cold War: crises, 1958-70
points: Rising tension: Berlin refugees and ultimatum, summit meetings, the Cuban Revolution and the Bay of Pigs.
Crises: the Berlin Wall (1961), the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Prague Spring.
Reactions: Kennedy in West Berlin, the hotline, arms-control treaties and the Brezhnev Doctrine.

units.title: Superpower relations and the Cold War: end of the Cold War, 1970-91
points: Detente: SALT 1, the Helsinki Accords and SALT 2.
End of detente: Afghanistan, the Carter Doctrine, Olympic boycotts, Reagan's SDI.
Collapse of Soviet control, 1985-91: Gorbachev's new thinking, fall of the Berlin Wall, end of the Warsaw Pact.

units.title: Early Elizabethan England: Queen, government and religion, 1558-69
points: Elizabeth's accession: legitimacy, gender, marriage and financial, religious and French pressures.
The 1559 religious settlement and the Church of England.
Puritan and Catholic challenges.
Mary, Queen of Scots and her relations with Elizabeth, 1568-69.

units.title: Early Elizabethan England: challenges at home and abroad, 1569-88
points: Plots and revolts: Northern Earls, Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington; Walsingham's spies.
Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587.
Spain: rivalry, privateering and Drake.
War 1585-88: the Netherlands, Dudley and the Cadiz raid.
The Armada: invasion plans, key events and reasons for English victory.

units.title: Early Elizabethan England: society in the Age of Exploration, 1558-88
points: Education and leisure, including sport and theatre.
The problem of the poor: rising poverty, vagabondage and changing policy.
Exploration: new technology, trade and Drake's circumnavigation.
Attempted colonisation of Virginia: Raleigh's role and reasons for failure.

units.title: Weimar and Nazi Germany: the Weimar Republic, 1918-29
points: Origins 1918-19: unrest, the Kaiser's abdication, armistice and strengths and weaknesses of the Constitution.
Early challenges, 1919-23: stab-in-the-back myth, Versailles, Spartacists, Freikorps, Kapp Putsch, hyperinflation and the Ruhr.
Golden Years 1924-29: Stresemann, Rentenmark, Dawes and Young Plans, Locarno and the League.
Changes in society: living standards, women and culture.

units.title: Weimar and Nazi Germany: Hitler's rise to power, 1919-33
points: Early Nazi Party, 1920-22: Hitler's early career, the Twenty-Five Point Programme and the SA.
Munich Putsch and the party 1923-28: consequences, Mein Kampf, limited support and the Bamberg Conference.
Growth of support, 1929-32: unemployment, the Communists, propaganda and the SA.
Becoming Chancellor, 1932-33: the 1932 elections and the roles of Hindenburg and von Papen.

units.title: Weimar and Nazi Germany: Nazi control and dictatorship, 1933-39
points: Creating a dictatorship: Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives and Hitler becoming Fuhrer.
Police state: Gestapo, SS, concentration camps and control of the legal system.
Controlling attitudes: Goebbels, propaganda, media, rallies, the 1936 Olympics, culture and the churches.
Opposition, resistance and conformity, including Niemoller, Swing Youth and Edelweiss Pirates.

units.title: Weimar and Nazi Germany: life in Nazi Germany, 1933-39
points: Policies towards women: family, marriage, employment and appearance.
Policies towards the young: Hitler Youth, League of German Maidens and education.
Employment and living standards: labour service, autobahns, rearmament, Labour Front, Strength Through Joy.
Persecution of minorities: Slavs, Roma and Sinti, homosexuals, disabled people and Jewish people (1933 boycott, Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht).

commandWords.meaning: Give causes or reasons, linked and supported with knowledge
Tell the sequence of events, linking cause and consequence
Judge a source's value using content, provenance and context
Weigh evidence for and against a view and reach a judgement
Draw a supported conclusion from a source
Break down a situation to show how parts connect

skills: Use second-order concepts: cause, consequence, change, continuity, similarity, difference, significance
Infer from and evaluate sources for utility using content, provenance and context
Analyse and evaluate historical interpretations and why they differ
Write extended, line-of-argument answers with supported judgement
Build accurate chronology and secure knowledge of period, theme and place
Use accurate spelling, punctuation, grammar and specialist terms (SPaG marks)

links.topic: Urban issues and challenges: Whitechapel and inner-city change
links.how: History studies Victorian overcrowding and crime; Geography studies urbanisation, inequality and regeneration

links.topic: 1854 Soho cholera outbreak and John Snow's mapping
links.how: History gives the public-health context; Geography teaches mapping disease; Science explains water-borne infection

links.topic: Forensic science and DNA in policing
links.how: Biology explains fingerprints and DNA; History traces how science changed detection

links.topic: Nuclear fission and the atomic bomb
links.how: Physics explains the fission reaction; History explains its effect on superpower relations

links.topic: Changing economic world: Cold War, aid and global trade
links.how: History covers the Marshall Plan and blocs; Geography covers aid, development and trade links
English analyses persuasive language; History applies it to Goebbels, rallies and media
Maths shows how hyperinflation grows; History explains its causes and effects

links.topic: Exploration, trade and colonisation: Drake and Virginia
links.how: Geography gives navigation and global trade patterns; History explains motives and failure
RE covers beliefs and divisions; History covers the 1559 settlement and religious challenges

links.how: History records persecution and Conscientious Objectors; RE and Citizenship discuss justice and rights
D&T looks at instruments and design; History shows their role in exploration and propaganda

contextNote: Several units (witch-hunts, persecution of minorities, Nazi dictatorship) need accurate, evidence-based teaching. Teach what happened, who was affected and why historians judge it as they do; the exam asks for explanation and evaluation, not endorsement of any view.
gaps: AO descriptions are paraphrased in general terms; only the AO weightings (overall and per paper) were read from the specification text.

Option-code discrepancy to resolve: the school's lesson files label Crime and punishment as 'option 11' and Weimar and Nazi Germany as 'option 32'. In the Pearson specification text read, Crime and punishment with Whitechapel is option 10 (option 11 is Medicine in Britain) and Weimar and Nazi Germany is option 31 (option 32 is Mao's China). Correct the lesson files or confirm entry codes.

Option choice is inferred from the lesson files (Y10 crime and Whitechapel pairing; Cold War, Elizabethan England and Weimar named as the school's set). Confirm the final entry options with the exams officer.
Year 10 and 11 lessons cover only Crime c1000-c1500 and Hitler's rise (Key Topic 2) so far; the rest of each option is placed by recommended sequence.

Available options not taught: Paper 1 options 11 Medicine in Britain with the British sector of the Western Front, 12 Warfare and British society with London and the Second World War, 13 Migrants in Britain with Notting Hill.

Available options not taught: Paper 2 period studies P1 Spain and the New World, P2 British America 1713-83, P3 The American West, P5 Conflict in the Middle East 1945-95; British depth studies B1 Anglo-Saxon and Norman England, B2 Richard I and John, B3 Henry VIII and his ministers. Any period study pairs with any depth study.
Available options not taught: Paper 3 options 30 Russia and the Soviet Union 1917-41, 32 Mao's China 1945-76, 33 The USA 1954-75.

Pearson notes option changes taking effect for assessment from summer 2026 (options 10-13, B1-B4, P1, P2, P4, 30-33); the exact changes were not itemised in the text read and should be checked against Pearson's update notice.
Pearson's command-word glossary was not in the text read; command words listed are those used in Edexcel papers and need checking against past papers.

Pearson's SPaG total: two statements of up to 4 marks (Paper 1 Section B, Paper 3 Question 3d) were read; paper totals of 52, 64 and 52 sum to 168 and the exact SPaG allocation within them should be confirmed.
